tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md shows the startup and peak-RSS tables exactly as quoted against pinned wasmtime 43.0.1, wazero 1.11.0, wasmer 5.0.4 and WasmEdge 0.16.1; the harness is public (scripts/run_bench.sh with hyperfine 5 runs + 3 warmup, fixtures under bench/runners, comparators pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench), zwasm is built with Zig 0.16.0 (pinned in flake.nix) at -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, and the host is an Apple M4 Pro.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: zwasm built with Zig 0.16.0 (pinned in flake.nix) via zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; comparators wasmtime 43.0.1, wazero 1.11.0, wasmer 5.0.4, WasmEdge 0.16.1 pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup; peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
corrections.caveats: The win is cold-start latency and memory footprint only. The same doc shows the optimizing JITs ahead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; matrix 343 vs 88 ms; base64 781 vs 57 ms, about 13.7x). The startup rows time a whole process (spawn + instantiate + run) on sub-10 ms guests, so they measure startup, not execution; the zwasm-aot row excludes its one-off compile step while comparator rows include their JIT compile, and the doc does not say whether wasmtime/wasmer compilation caches were on. Single host (Apple M4 Pro, macOS); wasmer only on aarch64-darwin. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, zwasm v2.7.0 with the JIT compiled out) puts zwasm's interpreter at a geomean 8.47x the fastest runtime's CPU time on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, WasmEdge 8.42). A fork's README (andypeng2015/zwasm) says the 'majority match or beat wasmtime' on 29 benchmarks, which the canonical benchmarks doc does not support. github.com/clojurewasm/zwasm (used by the rebecker harness) appears to be the project's earlier home. v1 line (frozen at v1.11.1) is MIT; v2 is Apache-2.0. Embeddable from C/C++ via the standard wasm-c-api.

notes: Numbers match docs/benchmarks.md exactly; repo 186 stars, Apache-2.0, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-05. Shortcoming: only startup and RSS wins; 1.5-13.7x slower than wasmtime on sustained compute, and the interpreter is about 8.5x off the fastest interpreter in an independent harness.

tier_reason: Independent shootout by the libsodium author (jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2021-Q1) runs WAVM against wasmtime, wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift, Singlepass), Node.js/V8 and Lucet with public benchmark code (libsodium 1.0.18-stable dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench) and per-test raw logs, LLVM 11.1.0 and wasm-opt -O4 named; the CPU model is never stated ('machines with an Intel CPU', 'my laptop'), so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text (macOS x86_64): 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test' and 'about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); V8 (Node.js) second; Lucet slowest. Total-time chart (summed from the per-test logs in 2021-Q1/output/macos-x86_64, derived from page data): wavm 4.63, node 5.23 (1.13x wavm), wasmer-llvm 5.44 (1.17x), wasmtime 6.65 (1.43x), wasmer-cranelift 10.70, wasmer-jit 10.98, wasmer-singlepass 11.11, lucet 11.61 (2.5x), native 2.04 (sums of the logged per-test times in units of 1e12; the chart plots the same totals rescaled). Per-test geomean of time vs wavm (derived from page data, 58 tests): wasmtime 1.47x, node 1.20x, wasmer-llvm 1.09x, lucet 2.47x, wasmer-singlepass 2.56x. Linux x86_64 LLVM-runtime run: 'wavm remains undethroned, but SSVM comes really close'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: All runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js from stock binaries); libsodium 1.0.18-stable built with LLVM 11.1.0 (Homebrew) via ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; native and WebAssembly builds use the same default optimization flags; runtimes invoked through libsodium's test/default/wasi-test-wrapper.sh.
corrections.caveats: Data are from February 2021 on an unnamed Intel macOS laptop plus an unnamed Linux x86_64 machine; WAVM was not run on ARM. The 'every single test' sentence is contradicted by the raw logs: wasmer-llvm beat WAVM on 16 of 58 macOS tests (mostly within 5%, auth3 at 0.46x and box2 at 0.83x of WAVM's time), so WAVM wins the totals, not every test. Reported times exclude module compilation/initialization, so WAVM's LLVM compile cost is not counted. The 2022-12 round in the same repo did not include WAVM (res/ has no wavm.csv), the repo was archived 2026-08-19, and the 2023 and 2026 posts on 00f.net are blocked here; a search snippet for the 2026 post says wasmer is the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, and that WAVM has the best optimizer (snippet only). WAVM's last commit is 2026-04-04 (a burst of fixes that day); its pace is slow.

notes: Real independent evidence; ranking in the record was off (wasmtime beats wasmer-singlepass in the chart) and the 'every single test' quote is overstated per the raw logs, both corrected. Shortcomings: 2021-era data, CPU model unstated, wasmer-llvm faster on 16 of 58 tests, 2026 rerun reportedly puts wasmer ahead (snippet only).

tier_reason: The README Performance section carries the quoted PolyBench/C slowdown table (Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js+Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%) with no hardware, versions or flags; the repo's code_benches/run.py only compares native against aWsm variants, and the peer-reviewed Sledge (Middleware 2020) and eWASM (EMSOFT 2020) papers holding the methodology are unreachable here (www2.seas.gwu.edu and par.nsf.gov EGRESS_BLOCKED), so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the cross-runtime comparison. The repo's code_benches/run.py (native vs aWsm only) builds native code with clang -O3 and Wasm with wasi-sdk/wasmception clang -O3 -flto, then compiles aWsm's LLVM bitcode with clang -O3.
corrections.caveats: README says 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README. A search snippet (snippet only) says the Middleware 2020 Sledge paper holds the same x86-64 comparison with Wasmer v0.12.0, WAVM v0.0.0-prerelease and Lucet v0.4.1, and that aWsm is within 1.1x of native on 24 of 30 PolyBench/C kernels; the paper itself was not reachable (a paper-access retier could move this to B). Wasmtime is absent from the x86-64 table, and all comparator versions are 2020-era. Microcontroller support: Arm's bento-linker README (an Arm collaborator of the aWsm group) measures aWsm on an nRF52840 (Cortex-M4, arm-none-eabi-gcc -Os -flto -mcpu=cortex-m4, compiler version not stated) at 78,896 ns vs 132,688 ns for WAMR AOT and 2,079,359 ns for wasm3 on qsort, and 6,823,538 ns vs 12,368,716 ns (WAMR AOT) and 157,946,032 ns (wasm3) on maze. Rust compiler plus C runtime: only the generated objects and runtime are linked into C/C++ programs. The 2026-07-13 last commit is a submodule bump; the previous code change was 2025-11-19 and the README pins Rust 1.56.0, so development is slow.

notes: README numbers match exactly; repo 353 stars, BSD-3-Clause, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-13 (submodule bump). Shortcomings: 2020-era first-party numbers without methodology in the repo, no Wasmtime row, comparator harness not public; peer-reviewed paper blocked here.
